subject: Chemistry
description: Reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, Kc/Kp

questions.stem: At chemical equilibrium, the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are:

options.option_text: Both equal to zero, so the reaction stops completely
Equal to each other, so concentrations stay constant
Forward rate is faster than the reverse rate value
Reverse rate is faster than the forward rate value

questions.explanation: DYNAMIC equilibrium — molecular reactions continue in both directions, but rates are equal so net concentrations don't change. Equilibrium ≠ stopping. Distractor 1 — common misconception; reactions DO continue. Distractors 3 and 4 describe non-equilibrium states (where reaction proceeds in one net direction).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: LE CHATELIER'S PRINCIPLE states that a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by:

options.option_text: Speeding up both reactions until the disturbance is gone
Shifting in a direction that opposes the change applied
Reaching a new equilibrium with the same constant value
Producing only the original reactants and no products

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier (1884): if a system in equilibrium is disturbed (change in concentration, temperature, or pressure), it shifts in the direction that opposes the disturbance, restoring a new equilibrium. Examples: increase reactant → forward shift; remove product → forward shift; increase pressure → shift to side with fewer moles of gas; raise temperature → shift in endothermic direction. Distractor 3 false because Kc CAN change with temperature.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: For the reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (exothermic), increasing the TEMPERATURE will:

options.option_text: Shift equilibrium toward more ammonia formation
Shift equilibrium back toward N₂ and H₂ reactants
Have no effect because Kc remains exactly constant
Cause both reactions to halt completely at higher heat

questions.explanation: Forward reaction is EXOTHERMIC (releases heat). Raising temperature ADDS heat → equilibrium shifts in the ENDOTHERMIC direction (consumes heat) → REVERSE direction → less ammonia, more N₂ and H₂. Industrial Haber-Bosch process compromises: moderate temperature (~450 °C — high enough for adequate rate but not so high that equilibrium goes backwards), high pressure (~200 atm — pushes forward by Le Chatelier since 4 mol gas → 2 mol). Iron catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse equally.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: Adding a CATALYST to a reaction at equilibrium will:

options.option_text: Shift equilibrium toward more products being formed
Help equilibrium be reached faster without shifting position
Increase the equilibrium constant for the forward step
Decrease both forward and reverse reaction rates equally

questions.explanation: A catalyst speeds up FORWARD AND REVERSE reactions equally → equilibrium reached faster, but POSITION of equilibrium (Kc) is UNCHANGED. Catalyst does not appear in the equilibrium expression. Industrial significance: catalysts make commercial-scale reactions feasible by reducing the time to reach equilibrium, even though they can't change the maximum yield. Distractor 1 false. Distractor 3 — catalysts don't change Kc. Distractor 4 — they INCREASE rates, not decrease.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: For the reaction A(g) + B(g) ⇌ 2C(g), if the volume of the container is HALVED (pressure doubled), equilibrium will:

options.option_text: Shift toward the products since they have more atoms
Stay in place since the moles of gas are equal on both sides
Shift toward the reactants since they were given first
The forward and reverse rates both fall to zero now

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier and pressure: equilibrium shifts toward the side with FEWER moles of gas when pressure is increased. Here both sides have 2 moles of gas (1+1 reactants vs 2 products) → no shift. Example: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is also pressure-insensitive. CONTRAST: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ has 4 → 2 moles → high pressure favours products (forward).
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: If the equilibrium constant Kc for a reaction is VERY LARGE (e.g., 10⁶), it means at equilibrium:

options.option_text: Reactants are present in much larger amounts than products
Products are formed almost completely from the reactants
The reaction proceeds equally in both directions still
The reaction has not started since rate is far too low

questions.explanation: Kc = [products]^stoich / [reactants]^stoich. Large Kc → numerator (products) >> denominator (reactants) → equilibrium lies far toward the products. Practical implication: reaction is essentially complete (e.g., combustion reactions have Kc ~10⁴⁰, considered to 'go to completion'). Small Kc (<<1) → equilibrium lies toward reactants; very little product forms. Kc ≈ 1 → comparable amounts of both. Note: Kc only describes the equilibrium position, NOT the rate.
questions.subject: Chemistry

questions.stem: If we DOUBLE the concentration of one of the reactants in a reversible reaction at equilibrium, the system will:

options.option_text: Shift the equilibrium backward to undo the addition
Shift forward to consume the added reactant gradually
Halt all reaction since equilibrium is now disturbed
Decompose into the original elements automatically

questions.explanation: Le Chatelier: adding more reactant → forward reaction speeds up (relative to reverse) until a NEW equilibrium is reached, with more products formed. Some of the added reactant gets consumed; final concentration of reactant is higher than original equilibrium but lower than the disturbed value. Industrial principle: removing product (or adding reactant) keeps reaction going; this is exploited in continuous processes. Distractor 1 reverses direction. Distractor 3 — equilibrium doesn't HALT. Distractor 4 — false.
